claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: Rarity precedes extinction
claims.statement: Species generally become rare before they become extinct, as seen in recent Tertiary formations and in animals exterminated by humans.

operationalizations.text: Measure trends in site occupancy, geographic range size, and specimen abundance in the time bins immediately preceding a species' last appearance in Cenozoic fossil databases and historical conservation records.

Estimate occupancy or abundance trajectories before last appearance in fossil species and before documented modern extinctions. Test whether declining rarity occurs more often than stable or increasing abundance immediately before extinction.

Compare occupancy or occurrence counts in the interval before last appearance with counts for species that survive the same interval. A drop confined to the species that are about to disappear would support the claim; extinction from high occupancy would count against it.

obstacles: Declining abundance immediately before last fossil appearance is partially confounded by the Signor-Lipps truncation effect unless sampling-standardized occupancy models are used.
The Signor-Lipps effect can manufacture apparent pre-extinction rarity.
Occurrence counts are imperfect abundance proxies.
The Signor-Lipps effect produces a spurious decline in records before the last appearance.
Most fossil collections record presence, so rarity is occupancy rather than population size.
Historical cases of human extermination are documented piecemeal and are not one abundance series.

claims.label: Horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra descend from a striped common ancestor
claims.statement: The domestic horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra are descended from a common ancestor that was striped like a zebra, which explains the occasional appearance of stripes in horses, asses and their hybrids.

operationalizations.text: Perform ancestral state reconstruction of coat striping patterns across a time-calibrated whole-genome phylogeny of extant and extinct *Equus* species (horses, asses, hemiones, zebras, quagga) and perform haplotype-sharing/introgression and developmental genetic analyses of the *TBX3* locus controlling dun primitive markings and stripes across equids.

Infer Equus relationships and reconstruct ancestral coat-pattern states using ancient and modern genomes, preserved pigmentation loci, fossil evidence and extant phenotype coding. A common ancestor with high posterior support for striping supports the claim; independent stripe origins or a confidently unstriped ancestor refute it.

Estimate the phylogeny of living and recently extinct equids from genomes and reconstruct the striping state of their common ancestor. A single clade whose ancestor is reconstructed as striped would confirm the claim; an unstriped ancestor, or striping confined to nested zebra lineages, would refute the striped-parent clause. Common ancestry itself is a separate and sharper test than the stripe reconstruction.

obstacles: Ancestral state reconstruction on extant tip states alone has wide confidence intervals at the root of *Equus*, though combining phylogenomics with the functional evolutionary genetics of the ancestral *TBX3* dun/striping regulatory allele resolves whether striping machinery is ancestral vs derived.
Coat stripes are rarely preserved in fossils.
Ancient DNA does not reach the deepest Equus common ancestor and pigmentation genotype-phenotype mapping is incomplete.
Striping is evolutionarily labile, so ancestral-state reconstruction can be equivocal.
The phenotype of stem equids is inferred rather than observed.
Partial leg and shoulder stripes in horses and asses can be coded in more than one way.

claims.label: Species of larger genera more often present varieties
claims.statement: Within a country, a larger proportion of the species in larger genera present varieties than of the species in smaller genera, and those that vary have on average more varieties.

operationalizations.text: Split genera within regional and global floras and beetle faunas into large versus small genera (or model genus species richness continuously), and test whether species in larger genera have a higher probability of having named infraspecific varieties/subspecies and a higher mean number of varieties per variable species.

Within regions and major clades, regress the proportion of species with accepted varieties and varieties per varying species on genus species richness, controlling sampling effort. A consistent positive relationship supports the claim; zero or negative effects refute it.

Within each country or regional biota, compare the proportion of species that have named varieties, and the mean number of varieties, between species in genera above and below the median genus size. Higher proportions and means on the large-genus side, after controlling for study effort, would support the pattern; a null or reversed difference would refute it.

obstacles: Genus circumscriptions and splitting/lumping philosophies vary among taxonomic schools, though phylogenetic genera can also be used as a robustness check.
Taxonomic effort is greater in species-rich genera.
Variety rank is used unevenly among clades.
Variety rank is used inconsistently and is often omitted from global checklists.
Large genera are studied more intensively, so they accumulate more named varieties.
Beetle faunas, part of the original scope, are less consistently digitized than vascular-plant floras.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.label: Thick fossil-rich formations accumulate during subsidence
claims.statement: Fossiliferous formations thick and extensive enough to survive later erosion are formed in shallow seas during periods of slow subsidence in which the supply of sediment roughly keeps pace with sinking.

operationalizations.text: Test across geological columns whether thick, laterally extensive, richly fossiliferous shallow-marine formations occur predominantly in basins undergoing tectonic/thermal subsidence where accommodation space creation matches sediment supply, by cross-referencing formation thickness, paleobathymetry/facies, and fossil richness.

Relate formation thickness, fossil richness, depositional depth, tectonic subsidence histories, and sediment accumulation rates. Concentration of thick fossil-rich units in slowly subsiding shallow basins with accommodation matched by sediment supports the mechanism.

Relate formation thickness and fossil richness in shallow-marine units to independent evidence of subsidence, such as tectonic setting and backstripping, not to thickness alone. A positive association during slow subsidence with sediment keeping pace would support the claim; thick fossil-rich sections formed mainly during uplift or non-depositional deepening would count against it.

obstacles: Eustatic sea-level rise can also create shallow-marine accommodation space over shorter timescales, though accumulating *thick* (hundreds to thousands of meters) shallow-marine sequences that survive subsequent erosion requires crustal subsidence.
Present thickness reflects compaction and later erosion.
Subsidence histories require regional models.
Thickness is often used to infer subsidence, which makes the association partly circular.
Independent tectonic evidence is uneven outside well-studied basins.
The wording 'all our ancient formations' is stronger than any basin sample.

claims.label: Probably all organisms descend from one primordial form
claims.statement: By analogy, probably all organisms that have ever lived on earth have descended from a single primordial form.

operationalizations.text: Apply formal statistical tests of Universal Common Ancestry (UCA, e.g. Theobald's likelihood ratio / AIC test and tree-congruence tests across universally conserved translational/transcriptional proteins and optimality of the universal genetic code) comparing a single primordial origin (LUCA) against multiple independent origins of Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.

Test universal common ancestry against multiple-origin models using conserved molecular machinery, near-universal genes, the genetic code and rare shared features while accounting for horizontal transfer. Strong likelihood or model-selection support for one connected ancestry supports the claim.

Test whether all extant organisms, and fossils that can be placed, share homologous core genes and a single rooted network of descent. The claim is confirmed for known life if those cores are universal and congruent, and refuted if a lineage has an unrelated genetic system; organisms that left no descendants remain outside the test.

obstacles: Extinct pre-LUCA stem lineages that left no surviving descendants cannot be directly sampled, though UCA of all known cellular life is directly testable.
Extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in early cellular evolution requires modeling reticulation alongside vertical descent.
The earliest signal is obscured by horizontal gene transfer and sequence saturation.
All organisms that ever lived cannot be sampled directly.
Gene exchange at the root is compatible both with one primordial cell and with a community of exchanging forms.
A second origin that died out without descendants would not appear in genomes or in the fossil record of later life.
Universal chemistry is expected under common ancestry and is also expected if early chemical options were severely limited.

claims.label: Identical alpine species on distant mountains are relicts of the Glacial period
claims.statement: The same arctic and alpine species on widely separated mountain summits and in arctic regions are relicts of populations that spread across the intervening lowlands during the Glacial period and were stranded on mountains and in the far north as the climate warmed.

operationalizations.text: Test whether disjunct arctic-alpine plant and animal populations across European and North American mountains occur as late Pleistocene fossils in intervening lowlands and exhibit shallow coalescent divergence times (dating to the Last Glacial Maximum / Holocene transition) in population-genetic datasets.

Combine dated pollen and fossil occurrences with population genomics and species distribution models to test lowland range continuity during glacial maxima and subsequent isolation on mountains and in the Arctic. Competing preglacial vicariance or independent colonization should predict different dates and routes.

For arctic-alpine species shared among separated mountains and the Arctic, test whether last-glacial fossils occur in the intervening lowlands and whether genetic data show one recent northern population. Deep divergence among summit populations, together with no glacial-age lowland fossils, would count against a glacial-relict origin.

obstacles: Some alpine disjuncts result from recent post-glacial long-distance dispersal rather than continuous lowland vicariance, requiring coalescent demographic models to distinguish the two.
Pollen often resolves only to genus.
Many species have idiosyncratic glacial refugia.
Pollen and many macrofossils are not identified to species.
Range-wide genetic studies cover a subset of the European and North American biota.
Survival on unglaciated peaks and later long-distance dispersal can mimic parts of the relict pattern.

claims.label: Regions sharing many allied species will also share some identical species
claims.statement: Wherever two regions, however distant, contain many closely allied or representative species, they will also contain some identical species and many doubtful forms ranked variously as species or varieties, showing past migration between them.

operationalizations.text: Across pairs of non-adjacent biogeographic regions or floristic/faunistic provinces, test whether pairs sharing a high number of sister species or congeneric endemics ('representative species') also share at least some identical native species and elevated proportions of subspecies/infraspecific taxa.

Across pairs of regions, quantify counts of close phylogenetic replacements and test whether those counts predict shared species after controlling for area, distance and sampling. A reliably positive association supports the prediction; region pairs with many allied forms but no shared species refute its universal wording.

Across pairs of bioregions, count shared species, sister or congeneric pairs, and taxa with unstable species-versus-variety rank, then test whether regions rich in allied pairs also share some identical species and more borderline taxa. The claim is confirmed if that joint pattern is nearly general after controlling for region size and survey effort, and refuted if many region pairs have numerous allied species and no shared species.

obstacles: Taxonomic philosophy (splitting vs. lumping across regional floras and faunas) directly affects whether populations in two regions are scored as identical species, subspecies, or distinct representative species.
Ancient vicariance (e.g. Gondwanan or Eastern Asian–Eastern North American disjunctions) can leave shared genera/sister clades after all identical species have diverged.
Species concepts and doubtful forms vary among taxonomic authorities.
Unequal inventory effort creates false absences.
Taxonomists already split and lump borderline forms most actively where regions share related biotas, so 'doubtful forms' partly reflect effort.
A few very widespread species can create shared-species counts without any special history of migration.
Survey effort and species concepts differ sharply between regions, which can manufacture or hide the predicted association.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.label: First appearance of a species in a formation usually marks immigration
claims.statement: When a marine species first appears partway through a formation, the most probable explanation is that it immigrated into that area at that time rather than originated there.

operationalizations.text: For marine fossil species whose local first appearance occurs mid-formation in a regional basin, test whether earlier fossil occurrences of the same species (or its immediate sister/ancestral population) exist in other geographic basins globally in the Paleobiology Database, indicating regional immigration (range expansion/environmental tracking) rather than in-situ origination.

For regional first appearances within formations, compare local first-occurrence dates with older occurrences elsewhere and use phylogeographic or occupancy models to classify immigration versus local origination. A majority with prior external records supports the claim.

For marine species whose first local occurrence is above the base of a formation, test whether older occurrences exist in other regions. A majority with earlier records elsewhere would support immigration as the usual explanation; a majority with no earlier record anywhere, in well-sampled groups, would favor local origin.

obstacles: Incomplete sampling outside well-studied basins (North America and Europe) can cause a global first appearance to be missed if the species originated in an under-sampled region, though comparing local FADs across multiple well-sampled basins directly measures diachrony and immigration.
The true source area may be unsampled.
Age uncertainty can reverse apparent first appearances.
Failure to find an older record elsewhere is weak evidence of in-situ origin because most regions are undersampled.
Many species are known from a single basin, so the test has no second locality.
Reworking and uncertain correlation can create false earlier occurrences.

claims.label: Cross fertility is largely governed by systematic affinity
claims.statement: The fertility of first crosses between species and of their hybrids is largely, though not strictly, governed by systematic affinity, so that species of distinct families never produce hybrids while closely allied species generally cross easily.

operationalizations.text: Regress first-cross success and F1 hybrid fertility against phylogenetic/genetic distance ($K_s$, patristic distance, or taxonomic rank from congeneric to interfamilial) across plant and animal crossing datasets; confirm a strong positive relationship with affinity (negative relationship with divergence distance) alongside substantial variance among closely related species pairs.

Regress first-cross and hybrid fertility on independently estimated phylogenetic distance across species pairs, allowing clade-specific effects. A strong negative but imperfect relationship supports the claim.

Regress first-cross success and hybrid fertility on genetic or phylogenetic distance. A strong positive relationship of isolation with distance, with residual scatter and with no hybrids between families, supports affinity as a large but not strict governor; no relationship, or frequent fertile crosses between distant families, would refute it.

obstacles: Historical 19th-century 'systematic affinity' was based on morphology rather than molecular divergence, though both morphological taxonomy and molecular divergence yield the same macro-pattern.
Cross-outcome data are incomplete and biased toward close relatives.
The categorical family-level assertion is difficult to sample comprehensively.
Crossing outcomes outside a few model clades are not in the same table as the distances.
Family rank is a human cutoff, so 'never between families' partly reflects how families were drawn.
Genetic distance is a proxy for the systematic affinity of 1859 classifications.

claims.label: No clear line separates species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences
claims.statement: No clear line of demarcation exists between species and sub-species, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences; they blend into one another in an insensible series.

operationalizations.text: Plot the distribution of pairwise genetic divergence (d_XY, Fst), morphological distance, and reproductive isolation across population pairs, varieties, subspecies, and congeneric species to test whether they form a continuous gradation ('grey zone of speciation') rather than discrete non-overlapping modes.

Compile genetic, morphological and reproductive distances from individuals through named varieties, subspecies and species, and test whether any universal discontinuity separates ranks. Continuous overlapping distance distributions support the claim; a robust cross-taxon gap refutes it.

Build distributions of genetic and phenotypic distance for pairs ranked as individual variants, varieties, subspecies, and species. A single overlapping continuum would support the absence of a clear line; a repeatable gap between adjacent ranks, stable across groups, would refute it.

obstacles: Uneven geographic sampling of intermediate populations can create an artificial appearance of a gap between taxa.
Taxonomic ranks are partly assigned using the same traits.
Different species concepts imply different boundaries.
Barcode libraries sample species much more densely than the variety-to-individual end of the series.
A gap in animals can coexist with overlap in plants, so the universal wording can fail in one kingdom and hold in another.
Rank labels are partly conventional, so the test recycles taxonomic practice unless distances are computed first and ranks applied after.
